docs.title: ⚙️ Configuration System
docs.text: The project’s configuration system is a three‑layered, type‑safe mechanism built on Pydantic that ensures all settings are valid, consistent, and easy to customize.

docs.title: Base configuration (conf/config.yaml)
docs.text:
• General, project‑wide defaults (I/O paths, caching, Ray, GPUs, etc.).
  • Metric‑specific overrides (conf/model/*.yaml)
  • One file per metric (CLIP, BLIP2, ImageReward, TIFA) to tweak only that metric’s fields.
  • Command‑line overrides
  • Instant updates via --section.key=value, requiring no file edits.

docs.title: 🗂️ Base Configuration (conf/config.yaml)
docs.text:
# Core parameters
input:
  path: data/raw/challenge_set.csv         # Input CSV path
  chunk_size: 10000                        #  Process input csv in chunks

output:
  path: data/processed/challenge_set_${model.type}.csv          # Output CSV - Dynamic naming

app:
  cache_dir: data/cache         # Local image caching
  ttl_days: 7
  max_connections: 100.         # Parallel downloads
  output_columns:               # Output CSV structure
    - url
    - caption
    - score
  use_ray: true                 # use distributed computing
  ray_workers: 8                # number of workers for ray
  annoy_index_name: annoy-clip  


# Model configuration
model: ...

Note the ${model.type} placeholder—your output filename will automatically include clip, blip2, etc.

docs.title: 🗂️ Metric-Specific Configurations
docs.text:
Located underconf/model/, each YAML defines only that metric’s extra fields and defaults:

conf/model/
├── clip.yaml          # CLIP scoring model
├── blip2.yaml         # BLIP-2 (itm/itc)
├── image_reward.yaml  # ImageReward preference model
└── tifa.yaml          # TIFA VQA scoring

Examples:

  • BLIP2-itc (blip2.yaml):
type: blip2
mode: itc
model_name: blip2_image_text_matching
precision: fp32
batch_size: 8
variant: pretrain
  • TIFA score (tifa.yaml):
type: tifa
question_generation_model: tifa-benchmark/llama2_tifa_question_generation
unifiedqa_model: allenai/unifiedqa-v2-t5-large-1363200
vqa_model: blip2-flant5xl
precision: fp16

docs.title: 📌 Command-Line Overrides
docs.text:
Any parameter—base or metric—can be overridden without editing files:

python main.py --model=clip --model.precision=fp16 --app.max_connections=32
  • Format: --section.key=value
  • Works for any field in your loaded config hierarchy.

docs.title: 📌 Validation & Safety
docs.text:
All configs are validated against Pydantic schemas in src/config/config_schema.py. This guarantees:

  • Required fields are present
  • Types (int, str, Literal) match
  • Constraints (e.g. output.path must include ${model.type}) hold

If validation fails, you’ll see a clear error at startup rather than a runtime crash.

Examples:

ImageRewardConfig

class ImageRewardConfig(BaseModel):
    """ImageReward model configuration."""
    type: Literal["image_reward"]
    model_name: str
    batch_size: int = 16
    precision: Literal["fp16", "fp32"] = "fp32"

BLip2Config

class BLIP2Config(BaseModel):
    """BLIP-2 model configuration."""
    type: Literal["blip2"]
    model_name: str
    mode: str
    precision: Literal["fp16", "fp32"] = "fp32"
    batch_size: int = 8
    variant: Literal["pretrain", "coco"] = "pretrain"

Initialization Flow

  • Load & validate base + metric configs
  • Apply CLI overrides
  • Instantiate the registered model class with the validated config
  • Error if no matching @register_model(...) is found

This ensures you can’t accidentally request an unsupported metric or supply invalid params.

docs.title: 📌 Model Configuration and Creation
docs.text:
Each model has a corresponding configuration schema (e.g., ClipConfig, BLIP2Config) and is registered using a decorator:

Example:

@register_model(ImageRewardConfig)  # Links config schema to model class
class ImageRewardModel:
    def __init__(self, config: ClipConfig):  # Guaranteed valid config
        self.precision = config.precision  # fp16/fp32
        self.tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(config.model_name)
        ...

Initialization Flow:

  1. Validate config against config (e.g. ImageRewardConfig) schema
  2. Instantiate model (e.g. ImageRewardModel) with validated parameters
  3. Reject unregistered models to prevent runtime failures

docs.title: 📍 Metrics
docs.text: Metric Speed GPU Mem Human Correlation Compositional Use Case CLIPScore ●●● ● ● ● First-pass filtering BLIP-2 ●● ●● ●● ●● Balanced quality/speed ImageReward ●● ● ●●● ● Human preference optimization TIFA ● ●●● ●●● ●●● Interpretability, compositionality

docs.title: 1. CLIPScore
docs.text:
CLiPScore computes the cosine similarity between CLIP text and image embeddings.

Strengths:

  • Fast, lightweight, easy to integrate/implement.

Weaknesses:

  • Tends to overlook spatial relationships, missing objects and subtle attributes.
  • Low fine-grained compositional accuracy.
  • Lack of interpretability.

Best case

  • Provides a very coarse/broad alignment score.
  • Can be used when computational cost is a concern.

docs.title: 2. BLIP-2 (itm/itc)
docs.text:
BLIP2-itm/itc includes a frozen image encoder and a language Q-Former transformer, trained with Image-Text Contrastive learning (ITC) and Image-Text Matching objectives. In ITC mode, BLIP‑2 generates embeddings for image and text that are trained to have high cosine similarity for true pairs. In ITM mode, BLIP‑2 uses a cross‑modal attention head that outputs a match probability (logit) indicating whether the pair is aligned.

Strengths:

  • Inherits CLIP-like alignment ability with richer modeling.
  • Captures more fine-grained details than CLIP.
  • Cross‑attention mechanism provides a more direct match signal.

Weaknesses:

  • Still suffers from coarse-level limitations.
  • Lack of interpretability.

Use case

  • Easy alternative to CLIP.
  • Broad/coarse compatibility checks.

docs.title: 3. ImageReward
docs.text:
ImageReward is a learned reward model using a BLIP encoder (ViT‑L image encoder + transformer text encoder) as backbone, with a small MLP head to regress to human preference scores.

Strengths:

  • Directly trained with human feedback; closely aligned with human judgments.
  • Implicitly learns both fidelity and aesthetic preferences.
  • Generally outperforms CLIP and BLIP‑2 scores as a filter.

Weaknesses:

  • Can inherit biases from annotators/datasets.
  • Encodes broad human preference factors beyond strict prompt fidelity.

Use case

  • Optimizing for human-preferred outputs.
  • Combine with other metrics for pure semantic faithfulness.

docs.title: 4. TIFA (VQA-based)
docs.text:
TIFA is a fine‑grained, interpretable faithfulness metric. Unlike embedding‑based scores, TIFA uses Visual Question Answering (VQA) to check consistency between the prompt and image.

Process: 1. Generate question–answer pairs from the prompt via an LLM. 2. Use a VQA model (e.g., BLIP‑2 or mPLUG) to answer those questions on the image. 3. Compute accuracy of VQA answers as the TIFA score.

Strengths:

  • Explicitly checks every relevant detail of the prompt.
  • Handles object counts, attributes, and spatial relations.
  • Correlates strongly with human judgments on faithfulness.
  • Focuses on factual coverage, not aesthetics.

Weaknesses:

  • Computationally intensive.
  • Quality depends on underlying VQA system.

Use case

  • Prioritize faithfulness to the prompt.
  • Detailed interpretability and high human correlation.
  • Best for prompts with multiple objects, relations, or numeric attributes.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
• Each metric trades off speed, memory, interpretability, and compositional accuracy.
  • CLIPScore & BLIP‑2 (ITC): fast screening, coarse alignment.
  • BLIP‑2 (ITM): calibrated match probability, still coarse.
  • ImageReward: strongest human‑preference signal.
  • TIFA: highest faithfulness, interpretability.

Practical approach: use CLIP/BLIP for initial filtering, then apply TIFA or ImageReward on top candidates for fine‑grained judgment.

docs.title: 🔄 Cyclic Verification
docs.text:
A powerful way to evaluate and reinforce cross‑modal alignment is to enforce cycle consistency:

  1. Start with an original text prompt T1.
  2. Generate an image I = Gen(T1).
  3. Caption that image to obtain T2 = Cap(I).
  4. Ideally, T2 should match T1.

Benefits of cyclic verification:

  • Reference‑free evaluation: No need for human‑written reference captions; the cycle itself provides supervision.
  • Modality gap mitigation: Aligns text‑to‑image and image‑to‑text mappings, ensuring semantic fidelity both ways.
  • Fine‑grained feedback: Any missing details or hallucinations become evident when T2 differs from T1.

docs.title: Applying Cycle Consistency in Our Pipeline
docs.text:
• Text → Image: Use a text‑to‑image model (e.g. Stable Diffusion) to compute I = Gen(T1).
  • Image → Text: Use a captioning model (e.g. BLIP‑2) to compute T2 = Cap(I).
  • Comparison: Measure similarity between T1 and T2, either at the token level (e.g., edit distance) or embedding level (e.g., cosine similarity).

This cyclic metric can be added as an optional post‑processing step to flag cases where the round‑trip reconstruction deviates significantly.

docs.title: Jina CLIP v2 for Long Captions
docs.text:
For our CLIPScore implementation, we adopt jinaai/jina-clip-v2, a contrastive vision‑language model specifically designed to handle long or truncated text inputs via Matryoshka representations and vector truncation. Jina CLIP v2 extends the maximum token length up to thousands of tokens (8192 in its text tower) by:

  1. Multi‑stage contrastive training on text–text and text–image pairs, including longer synthetic captions :contentReference.
  2. Matryoshka representations: Enables dynamic truncation of embedding dimensions (down to 64) to trade off performance vs. storage.
  3. High image resolution support (512×512) for better fine‑grain visual features.

docs.title: Image-text similarity Pipeline
docs.text:
Image‑text Similarity Pipeline

This project provides two optimized pipeline implementations for computing image‑text similarity scores:

  • ImageTextPipeline (Single‑Node, Async)
  • RayImageTextPipeline (Distributed, Ray)

Both share the same high‑level steps—CSV chunking, image download & cache, batched model scoring, metrics logging, and result output but differ in concurrency and resource distribution.

docs.title: Common Workflow
docs.text:
1. Configuration Load

  • Uses config_loader.load_config() to read & validate conf/config.yaml (base) + conf/model/*.yaml (metric‑specific) + CLI overrides.

2. Component Initialization

  • CSV Reader: ChunkedCSVReader for streaming large files. -Cache Manager: CacheManager with TTL based on app.cache_dir & app.ttl_days. -Model: Created via ModelFactory.create_model(config.model).
  • Logger & Metrics: setup_logger + MetricsLogger to track throughput, errors, GPU usage, and score distributions.
  • CSV Writer: CSVWriter outputs to output.path with dynamic ${model.type} replacement.

3. Process Loop

Iterate over CSV chunks → split into batches → download/cache images → load & validate → score via model → record & write results.

**3. Cleanup ** Close cache, writer; write metrics JSON & score distribution plot; flush logs.

docs.title: ImageTextPipeline
docs.text: Use The Async, Single‑Node Version when you need a simple setup on one machine. Ideal for development, experimentation, or small‑scale runs.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Async I/O: Uses asyncio + AsyncHTTPClient for concurrent downloads.
  • Batch Inference: Groups records into batches (config.model.batch_size) for efficient GPU usage.
  • Chunked Reading: Prevents OOM when loading very large CSVs.
  • Smart Caching: TTL‑based caching to avoid re‑downloads.
  • Robust Error Handling: Continues past failed downloads or corrupt images, logs counts.

docs.title: 1. Initialization
docs.text: pipeline = ImageTextPipeline(config)

docs.title: 2. Run
docs.text: asyncio.run(pipeline.run())

docs.title: 3. Per-chunk
docs.text:
• Download missing images (_precache_images)
  • Load images with thread‑pool (_load_images)
  • Validate & filter (_validate_images)
  • Score batch (_score_valid_records)
  • Write rows & update metrics (_format_batch_results)

docs.title: 4. Finalize
docs.text: cache.close(), writer.close(), metrics_logger.write_summary(), metrics_logger.save_score_distribution_plot()

docs.title: RayImageTextPipeline
docs.text:
Use The Distributed Ray Version for large‑scale, multi‑GPU/-node runs—ideal for processing tens to hundreds of millions of records in parallel.

Additional Features

  • Ray Tasks: Spawns app.ray_workers RayWorker actors, each with its own model instance.
  • Multi‑GPU Support: Distributes across app.num_gpus GPUs (one GPU per worker by default).
  • Optional Index Mode: If cache_dir/annoy_indices/ contains index data, switches to nearest‑neighbor lookups without any model inference.

docs.title: 🌐 Key Differences from Base Pipeline
docs.text: Feature Base Pipeline Ray Pipeline Processing Single-process async Distributed across workers Model Instances Single One per worker Resource Use Single GPU/CPU Cross-device/cluster Pre computed embeddings support No Yes

docs.title: 1. Initialization
docs.text:
pipeline = RayImageTextPipeline(config)
pipeline.run()

docs.title: 2. Ray Setup
docs.text:
• ray.init(num_gpus=config.app.num_gpus)
  • Create app.num_gpus workers via @ray.remote(num_gpus=1)

docs.title: 3. Processing
docs.text: For each CSV chunk: - Split into batches - Dispatch worker.score_batch.remote(batch) - ray.get() to collect results - Write & log via CSVWriter and MetricsLogger

docs.title: 4. Annoy Index Integration (optional)
docs.text:
Index Mode Detection

Pipeline switches to index mode when detects:

  • Annoy index file (.ann)
  • Embedding numpy array (.npy)
  • Metadata mapping (.jsonl)
  cache_dir/
  ├── annoy_indices/
  │   ├── clip_index.ann       # Binary index file
  │   └── clip_meta.jsonl      # URL-to-embedding ID mapping
  └── embeddings/
      └── clip_embs.npy        # Combined image-text embeddings

If found, score_batch uses _score_with_inde; else _score_with_inference.

docs.title: Configuration Hooks & Extension Points
docs.text:
• Batch Size: config.model.batch_size controls number of examples per GPU inference call.
  • Concurrency:
  • Single‑node: config.app.max_connections for HTTP client concurrency.
  • Ray: config.app.ray_workers and config.app.num_gpus.
  • Index Mode: Drop an Annoy index + embeddings into your cache_dir to bypass inference.
  • QA Models: The TIFA pipeline outputs extra columns (questions, correct_answers, model_answers) when model.type=tifa, handled automatically.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Single‑node CLIP, no Ray

python src/pipeline.py --model clip --app.use_ray=False

Single‑node with 4 GPUs

python src/pipeline3.py --model clip --app.num_gpus=4

Distributed ImageReward on 4 GPUs and 4 Ray workers

python src/pipeline3.py \ --model image_reward \ --app.use_ray=True \ --app.num_gpus=4 \ --app.ray_workers=4

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
1. Create and activate a new Conda environment:
conda create -n image-text-similarity python==3.10
activate image-text-similarity
  1. Install dependencies via the included script:
chmod +x setup.sh
 ./setup.sh

docs.title: How to run
docs.text:
Running the Pipeline

By default, the pipeline entry point is src/pipeline.py. You can select your model and override any config parameters on the command line.

python src/pipeline.py --model <MODEL>
  • Overrides use the syntax --section.key=value.
  • Replace with one of the supported types/metrics below. Model Flag Metric Description Example Config Overrides --model clip CLIPScore --model.precision fp16 --model blip2 BLIP2-itc/itm --model.batch_size 32 --model tifa TIFA VQA-based --model.precision fp16 --model image_reward Human preference score --model.batch_size 16

docs.title: Custom  Overrides
docs.text:
Configuration

By default, the pipeline loads settings from conf/config.yaml. Here’s a snippet of the key parameters:

docs.title: conf/config.yaml
docs.text:
input:
  path:       data/raw/challenge_set.csv
  chunk_size: 10000

output:
  path: data/processed/challenge_set_${model.type}.csv

app:
  cache_dir:       data/cache
  ttl_days:        7
  max_connections: 100
  output_columns:
    - url
    - caption
    - score
  use_ray:      true
  ray_workers:  4
  num_gpus:     4
  annoy_index_name: annoy-clip

model:
  type:          clip
  model_name:    openai/clip-vit-base-patch32
  precision:     fp32
  truncation:    true

You can override any of these by passing --section.key=value flags:

python src/pipeline.py --model blip2 \
    --model.precision=fp16 \
    --model.batch_size=32 \

For more info on configuration please see Configuration

docs.title: Output Structure
docs.text:
The code will create a directory with the following structure:

.
└── <MODEL>
    ├── challenge_set_<MODEL>.csv
    ├── metrics_<MODEL>json
    └── score_distribution_<MODEL>.png

where is the deployed similarity model.

  • CSV:challenge_set_<MODEL>.csvcontains your input rows plus a new score column.
  • JSON: metrics_<MODEL>.json logs timing, memory, stats, errors, etc
  • PNG: score_distribution_<MODEL>.png visualizes the score histogram.

For more info on logged metrics please see Logging

docs.title: Scaling & Distributed Processing
docs.text:
To leverage multiple GPUs and/or Ray workers for faster inference:

  1. Switch Ray on/off

Ray disabled (single process across GPUs):

python src/pipeline.py --model clip --app.use_ray=False

Ray enabled (distributed actors):

python src/pipeline.py --model clip --app.use_ray=True
  1. Specify number of GPUs
python src/pipeline.py --model clip --app.num_gpus=4
  1. Set Ray worker count
python src/pipeline.py --model clip \
  --app.use_ray=True \
  --app.ray_workers=8 \
  --app.num_gpus=4
